title: Animation in React
summary: Use motion to clarify interface changes while keeping interactions accessible and responsive.

subtopics.title: Choose what motion explains
subtopics.explanation: Motion should answer a question: did the panel open, where did this card move, or what changed? If an animation does not help someone understand the result, remove it. A sign on a road points toward a destination; motion should guide attention with the same restraint.

subtopics.title: Use CSS for simple transitions
subtopics.explanation: A CSS transition interpolates between style values when state changes. It suits color, opacity, and many transform changes. Keep the duration short and the final state readable. For a disclosure, also update `aria-expanded` so the state is available without relying on movement.

subtopics.title: Reach for a library deliberately
subtopics.explanation: A library can coordinate elements entering and leaving, shared layout movement, or sequences. It also adds code and concepts. Use it when coordination solves a real problem, not just because a demo looks polished. First confirm the library supports your React version and reduced-motion needs.

subtopics.title: Respect reduced motion
subtopics.explanation: Some people ask the operating system to reduce animation. Read the reduced-motion preference and remove large movement, parallax, or long transitions where possible. Keep the same information and controls available. A moving walkway should have a safe still path beside it.

subtopics.title: Keep performance and input responsive
subtopics.explanation: Prefer animating `transform` and `opacity`, which browsers can often handle without recalculating the whole layout. Avoid long animations that block a button or hide a result. Test on a slower device and keep keyboard interaction available throughout.

foundations.overview: Animation changes how an interface looks over time. A short transition can show that a panel opened or a card moved. CSS works well for simple changes. An animation library can coordinate entering, leaving, and layout. Respect reduced-motion preferences and keep controls usable while motion runs.
foundations.mentalModel: Motion is a signpost: it should point out a change and then get out of the way.
foundations.whyItMatters: Well-chosen motion helps people understand what changed. Excessive motion can delay tasks, distract users, or cause discomfort.
foundations.formalDefinition: UI animation is a timed change in visual properties that communicates state or spatial relationships.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser may animate opacity and transforms efficiently, while layout-changing properties can require more rendering work.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use CSS transitions for simple state changes and a motion library when enter, exit, or layout coordination is genuinely complex.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear feedback makes interactions feel responsive and helps people keep their place.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Keep animation state tied to UI state, honor reduced-motion settings, and avoid duplicating the same transition logic.
foundations.performanceImpact: Prefer transform and opacity for frequent motion, and measure on lower-powered devices.
commonMisconceptions: Motion should explain a change; many controls are clearer without it.
A smooth animation is always accessible
People may request reduced motion or be sensitive to movement.
Layout changes can make the browser recalculate nearby positions.

codeLab.title: Animate a state change
codeLab.instructions: Create a panel that expands and collapses with a short CSS transition. Keep the control usable while the animation runs.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Clicking the button changes the panel height smoothly.
hints: Break the task into state, event handling, and rendered feedback.
Keep the interface accessible with labels and meaningful button text.
